A frozen parameter is not necessarily a frozen neuron.

That distinction is the center of this audit.

HOPE uses its functional capacity to build Dispersed Elastic Fine-Tuning,
or DEFT. The motivating idea is attractive: consolidate redundant source
features, protect a high-capacity core, turn low-capacity structure into
plastic slack, and block target-driven slack from feeding back into the core.

The paper then makes a strong promise. Once the structural mask has been
applied, the core is said to experience zero dynamic deviation during target
fine-tuning.

There are two separate questions hidden inside that promise:

1. Which neurons are core at the moment the promise is invoked?
2. What state must remain fixed for a core neuron, as defined by Eq. 2, to be
   the same operator?

The paper gives three different answers to the first question. Its proof gives
a useful but narrower answer to the second.

The result is not that DEFT's structural mask does nothing. The mask supports a
real routing guarantee. The result is that this guarantee protects a selected
input route into downstream core neurons, not every component of every
complete core operator.

## Start with the strongest fair version

DEFT assigns each neuron a binary elasticity

$$
E_i\in\{0,1\},
$$

where core neurons use $E_i=0$ and slack neurons use $E_i=1$. For a weight from
upstream neuron $k$ to downstream neuron $j$, Eq. 28 applies the structural
mask

$$
M_{j,k}=
\begin{cases}
0,&E_{\mathrm{in},k}>0\text{ and }E_{\mathrm{out},j}=0,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

The target model starts from

$$
W_0=M\odot W_{\mathrm{source}}.
$$

Equation 29 then gates each weight gradient by the elasticity of its
destination neuron:

$$
g_t=E_{\mathrm{out}}\odot\nabla_W L_{\mathrm{target}}(W_t).
$$

If an upstream slack activation changes but its route into a downstream core
neuron is permanently zero, that changing signal contributes exactly zero to
that downstream core input.

`verified_fact` (`P10-NARROW-ROUTING-GUARANTEE`): under the declared mask,
destination gate, and routing assumptions, a severed slack-to-core weight stays
zero in the deterministic audit. This is a genuine and useful decoupling
property.

The scope words matter. The theorem would be stronger only if the mask and
gradient rule also froze every state component belonging to the complete
functional neuron in Eq. 2. They do not.

## Before proving stability, define the partition

A partition must specify:

- the scalar being thresholded;
- the network state at which it is measured;
- whether the threshold is global or layer-specific;
- the treatment of equality;
- the treatment of merged, removed, inactive, and terminal-survivor slots;
- the time at which the resulting elasticity is attached.

DEFT does not give one answer to that list. It gives three.

### Main-text trajectory-cost partition

Equations 24 through 27 assign a pruning cost when neuron $i$ is removed during
progressive encoding:

$$
J_{\mathrm{prune}}^{(i)}
=
\frac{N^{(i)}\lVert f_i\rVert_{\mathcal H}}
{E_b^{(i)}},
\qquad
E_b^{(i)}=E_a^{(i)}-\lVert f_i\rVert_{\mathcal H}.
$$

The paper collects valid trajectory costs across the network, takes one global
percentile, applies its numerical fallback, and defines

$$
E_i=
\begin{cases}
1,&J_{\mathrm{prune}}^{(i)}<J_{\mathrm{lock}},\\
0,&J_{\mathrm{prune}}^{(i)}\ge J_{\mathrm{lock}}.
\end{cases}
$$

`paper_claim` (`P10-TRAJECTORY-PARTITION`): the main-text rule thresholds a
history-dependent destruction cost. Its scalar depends on the active width and
remaining capacity at the step when that neuron is removed.

This is not a threshold on the neuron's current raw capacity. It is also not
defined on an active terminal survivor that never receives a removal event,
unless an additional convention is supplied.

### Appendix H per-layer capacity partition

Definition H.1 instead starts from one threshold for each layer:

$$
\mathcal N_{\mathrm{core}}^{(\ell)}
=
\left\{i:\lVert f_i\rVert_{\mathcal H^{(\ell)}}>
\tau^{(\ell)}\right\},
$$

$$
\mathcal N_{\mathrm{slack}}^{(\ell)}
=
\left\{j:\lVert f_j\rVert_{\mathcal H^{(\ell)}}\le
\tau^{(\ell)}\right\}.
$$

`paper_claim` (`P10-LAYER-THRESHOLD-PARTITION`): the Appendix H guarantees
assume per-layer thresholds on current functional capacities. Equality belongs
to slack.

The appendix does not prescribe how its layer-specific thresholds are obtained
from the main-text global percentile. In the deterministic audit we set

$$
\tau^{(A)}=2,
\qquad
\tau^{(B)}=4.
$$

These values are an explicit audit instantiation allowed by Definition H.1.
They are not thresholds reported by the paper and not an inferred conversion
from the paper's percentile hyperparameter.

### Algorithm 3 global current-capacity partition

Algorithm 3 uses a third sequence:

1. merge redundancies;
2. compute capacities of the current active neurons;
3. take one global capacity percentile;
4. freeze a neuron only if it is active and its current capacity is above that
   global threshold.

`paper_claim` (`P10-CURRENT-CAPACITY-PARTITION`): Algorithm 3 thresholds current
functional capacities globally after merging. That differs in both scalar and
scope from the other two rules.

The pseudocode does not specify a percentile interpolation convention. At the
declared 50th percentile, the audit uses a float64 median and averages the two
central values for an even count. That implementation choice is part of our
fixture, not a paper result.

## One fixture, three different rule outputs

The smallest useful witness has two layers and six active neurons:

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\text{layer A}&A0&A1&A2\\ \hline
\text{current capacity}&1&2&8
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\text{layer B}&B0&B1&B2\\ \hline
\text{current capacity}&3&4&5.
\end{array}
$$

The declared encoding trace removes two neurons from each layer and retains
one terminal survivor.

For layer A:

$$
J(A0)=\frac{3\cdot1}{10}=0.3,
\qquad
J(A1)=\frac{2\cdot2}{8}=0.5.
$$

For layer B:

$$
J(B0)=\frac{3\cdot3}{9}=1,
\qquad
J(B1)=\frac{2\cdot4}{5}=1.6.
$$

At percentile 50,

$$
J_{\mathrm{lock}}
=\operatorname{median}(0.3,0.5,1,1.6)
=0.75.
$$

The trajectory rule therefore calls A0 and A1 slack, and B0 and B1 core. A2
and B2 have no removal event in the declared trace, so the audit marks them
unassigned rather than inventing an Eq. 24 value.

The instantiated Definition H.1 rule calls only A2 and B2 core.

Algorithm 3 takes the global current-capacity threshold

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{global}}
=\operatorname{median}(1,2,3,4,5,8)
=3.5,
$$

and calls A2, B1, and B2 core.

The pairwise disagreement counts are:

$$
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
\text{comparison}&\text{disagreements}&\text{neurons}\\ \hline
\text{trajectory vs. layer threshold}&2&B0,B1\\
\text{trajectory vs. global current capacity}&1&B0\\
\text{layer threshold vs. global current capacity}&1&B1.
\end{array}
$$

The first two comparisons use the four neurons assigned by the trajectory
rule. The trajectory rule also leaves two terminal survivors outside its
observed-event domain.

`verified_fact` (`DEFT-PARTITION-MISMATCH`): the three printed specifications
threshold different quantities at different scopes. They disagree pairwise on
the four-neuron common assigned domain, while the trajectory rule leaves two
terminal survivors unassigned.

This is not a claim that one of the three rule outputs is empirically best. It is a
reproducibility result: Appendix H's guarantees cannot automatically transfer
to an inequivalent main-text or Algorithm 3 partition.

## What the structural proof actually protects

Theorem H.2 expands the input to a downstream core neuron into contributions
from upstream core and upstream slack subsets. Its dynamic argument uses two
facts:

1. destination-core weights and destination-core trainable parameters are
   frozen;
2. upstream-slack to downstream-core weights were set to zero and remain zero.

That proves a narrow statement about the signal entering downstream core.

The deterministic routing fixture makes the boundary visible. Let rows be
downstream destinations (core, slack) and columns be upstream sources (core,
slack):

$$
W_{\mathrm{source}}=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&3\\
5&7
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
M=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0\\
1&1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

After initialization,

$$
W_0=M\odot W_{\mathrm{source}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
5&7
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use raw gradient

$$
G=
\begin{bmatrix}
99&99\\
-2&-2
\end{bmatrix}
$$

and learning rate $\eta=0.5$. Destination elasticity zeroes the first row and
permits the second row to update:

$$
W_1=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&0\\
6&8
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now let the upstream activation vector change from

$$
h_0=[1,1]
\quad\text{to}\quad
h_1=[1,4].
$$

Before masking, the source core input is 5. Immediately after masking it is 2,
so the structural initialization shock has magnitude 3. During adaptation,
the downstream core input remains exactly 2 even though the upstream slack
activation changes.

The fixture therefore separates two quantities that should never be combined:

- static intervention shock: 3;
- post-mask dynamic slack-to-core interference: 0.

Theorem H.1 addresses the first with a capacity bound. Theorem H.2 addresses
the second under its assumptions. Neither number says that all state owned by
the upstream core operator is immutable.

## A core source can keep a plastic outgoing edge

Equation 2 defines a functional neuron using its complete outgoing vector:

$$
f_i(x)=g_i(x)\,w_{\mathrm{out},i}.
$$

In the routing fixture, the upstream core neuron's outgoing vector is the
first column of the weight matrix. It changes from

$$
w_{\mathrm{out},c}^{(0)}=[2,5]
\quad\text{to}\quad
w_{\mathrm{out},c}^{(1)}=[2,6].
$$

The core-to-core component stays frozen because its destination is core. The
core-to-slack component changes because Eq. 29 assigns elasticity by the
slack destination.

For a core activation with second moment
$\mathbb E[g_c^2]=1$, the operator capacities are

$$
\lVert f_c^{(0)}\rVert=\sqrt{29}
=5.385164807134504,
$$

$$
\lVert f_c^{(1)}\rVert=\sqrt{40}
=6.324555320336759.
$$

The exact operator-difference norm is 1, and the relative capacity change is
about 0.174440439.

`counterexample` (`P10-OUTGOING-OPERATOR-DRIFT`): destination-owned gradient
gating permits a core source neuron's outgoing component into slack to change.
Because Eq. 2 includes that component, the complete core source operator is
not immutable.

This does not contradict the narrow routing result. Both are true at once:
slack cannot enter downstream core through the severed route, while core can
still feed and adapt through downstream slack.

## Frozen trainables do not freeze BatchNorm state

BatchNorm running mean and variance are buffers. They change during training
mode through forward-pass state updates, not through the gradient multiplication
in Eq. 29.

The audit freezes every trainable scalar in a one-channel state machine:

$$
(w,b,\gamma,\beta)=(1,0,1,0).
$$

It starts with source buffers

$$
(\mu_0,v_0)=(0,1)
$$

and uses old-state momentum $r=0.5$:

$$
\mu_{t+1}=r\mu_t+(1-r)m_t,
\qquad
v_{t+1}=rv_t+(1-r)q_t.
$$

Two target batches provide declared moments

$$
(m_1,q_1)=(4,4),
\qquad
(m_2,q_2)=(6,9).
$$

The live buffers become

$$
(\mu_2,v_2)=(4,5.75).
$$

On fixed source probes $z=[-1,0,1]$ with
$\epsilon=10^{-5}$, the source-buffer output is approximately

$$
[-0.999995,0,0.999995],
$$

while the target-updated live-buffer output is approximately

$$
[-2.085142,-1.668114,-1.251085].
$$

Their root-mean-square difference is 1.7346960857596274. The trainable change
norm remains exactly zero.

`counterexample` (`P10-BN-BUFFER-DRIFT`): gradient masking alone does not make
the BatchNorm inference map immutable.

Appendix G.5 confirms the operational importance of this state: its source
retention protocol explicitly restores source BatchNorm moving statistics
before source evaluation.

`proposed_repair` (`P10-BN-STATE-REPAIR`): on the declared source probes,
freezing source buffers during target updates gives zero BatchNorm-output RMSE.
Explicit frozen or dual-tracked buffer ownership is a proposed policy; that
local control does not establish target-domain or trained-network performance.

## The complete Eq. 2 immutability claim fails twice

The two counterexamples are independent.

1. A core-to-slack outgoing weight can change because the destination is
   elastic.
2. A core BatchNorm buffer can change through target forward passes even when
   every trainable parameter is fixed.

`verified_fact` (`DEFT-CORE-DRIFT`): Theorem H.2's proof protects the selected
slack-to-core route, but does not freeze the complete Eq. 2 operator through
either of these state channels.

The precise correction is therefore:

> The structural mask can make downstream core inputs dynamically independent
> of upstream slack along the declared parameterized routes. It does not, by
> itself, make every complete core functional neuron immutable.

That narrower statement preserves the useful part of the theorem without
assigning it a larger state domain than the proof controls.

## A purged child is not yet a reusable vessel

DEFT also needs a state transition from compression to target adaptation.

The released-capacity narrative says that merging redundant core neurons
consolidates their feature into one parent and releases the other children as
plastic target capacity. Figure 4 depicts empty slots. Axiom 3 assigns released
children full plasticity. Proposition H.4 counts the freed parameter volume.

Algorithm 2, however, says that child $j$ is purged by removing it from the
layer.

`verified_fact` (`P10-PURGED-RELEASED-CONFLICT`): purging a child from the
active layer and exposing a reusable fixed-width plastic vessel are different
states. The paper does not specify
the transition that recreates or retains the slot, reconnects it, initializes
it, masks it, and registers it with the optimizer.

This is an under-specification, not a proof that released capacity cannot be
implemented. The missing state transition can be repaired explicitly.

## Keeping a completely zero slot is not enough

One tempting interpretation is to preserve tensor width but zero every
parameter belonging to the released child. That interpretation is not printed
by the paper, so the audit labels it as an independent test rather than a
paper-literal implementation.

Consider the scalar path

$$
s=\gamma ux+\beta,
\qquad
a=\operatorname{ReLU}(s),
\qquad
\hat y=va,
\qquad
L=\frac12(\hat y-y)^2.
$$

Use $x=y=1$ and the common convention
$\operatorname{ReLU}'(0)=0$. If

$$
u=\gamma=\beta=v=0,
$$

then $a=0$, the loss is 0.5, and every gradient is exactly zero. Direct SGD
leaves the slot at zero forever.

`counterexample` (`P10-DEAD-ZERO-SLOT`): a completely zeroed ReLU vessel is not
automatically plastic. Elasticity one cannot create a gradient where both
sides of the path are dead.

The result is scoped to the declared path and derivative convention. Bias,
normalization, skip routes, or explicit reinitialization can change the result.
That is precisely why the released-slot transition must be specified.

## A fixed-width repair can wake without an initial contribution

A minimal proposed repair keeps the logical slot but initializes its two sides
asymmetrically:

$$
u=1,
\qquad
\gamma=1,
\qquad
\beta=0,
\qquad
v=0.
$$

At initialization, the slot contributes zero because its outgoing coefficient
is zero. Its internal activation is live, so

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial v}=-1.
$$

After one SGD step with learning rate 0.25, $v=0.25$. A second backward pass
gives

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial v}=-0.75,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial u}
=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\gamma}
=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\beta}
=-0.1875.
$$

`proposed_repair` (`P10-FIXED-WIDTH-REPAIR`): on the declared scalar fixture,
a live incoming feature plus a zero outgoing coefficient preserves zero initial
contribution while allowing the slot to wake in two gradient steps.

A complete implementation still has to:

- keep every released-slot route into downstream core hard-masked;
- allow only slack or target-head destinations to become active;
- clear stale optimizer state for the reused slot;
- define BatchNorm affine and buffer initialization;
- record active/inactive status separately from elasticity;
- keep tensor shape and parameter ownership consistent across the transition.

Those are proposed implementation rules. They are not results reported by
HOPE v1.

## Source retention uses restored source state

Appendix G.5 does not evaluate source retention by sending source examples
through the untouched live target model.

It:

1. grafts the original source classification head back onto the adapted
   backbone;
2. masks connections from slack features into the source head;
3. restores source BatchNorm moving means and variances.

Algorithm 3 similarly constructs a source-evaluation state through
`MaskSlackDrift` before computing source validation accuracy.

`paper_claim` (`P10-SOURCE-STATE-RESTORATION`): the reported source protocol is
task-conditional state restoration, not a one-state evaluation of the live
target-adapted model.

The deterministic audit holds the source head and slack mask fixed and varies
only the BatchNorm policy:

$$
\begin{array}{l|c}
\text{source-evaluation buffer policy}&\text{source-probe RMSE}\\ \hline
\text{live target-updated buffers}&1.7346960857596274\\
\text{restore source buffers at evaluation}&0\\
\text{freeze source buffers during adaptation}&0.
\end{array}
$$

The zeroes are exact fixture equalities, not accuracy results. The comparison
shows why the policy changes what function is evaluated.

Restoration is a legitimate experimental protocol if it is reported as such.
But it carries task-specific state: a source head, a source mask, and source BN
buffers. It therefore cannot simultaneously serve as evidence that source
retention requires no task-specific evaluation state.

Freezing core buffers or maintaining explicitly named source and target buffer
tracks are possible repairs. Their target-domain consequences require real
experiments and are not inferred from this fixture.

## What survives, what fails, and what needs repair

The audit supports a more precise DEFT state machine.

What survives:

- `paper_claim`: DEFT proposes capacity-informed stability and plasticity.
- `verified_fact`: Eq. 28 can permanently sever a declared slack-to-core route.
- `verified_fact`: with destination-core trainables frozen, changing upstream
  slack does not dynamically enter the downstream core through that route.
- `paper_claim`: source evaluation restores source-specific state.

What does not survive as written:

- `verified_fact`: the three printed partition procedures are inequivalent.
- `counterexample`: frozen trainables do not freeze BatchNorm buffers.
- `counterexample`: destination gating permits core-to-slack outgoing drift.
- `verified_fact`: a child purged from the active layer is not yet an executable
  reusable slot.
- `counterexample`: a completely zeroed ReLU slot can be gradient-dead.

What remains proposed:

- choose one partition rule and bind the guarantee to it;
- keep fixed-width logical slots through transfer;
- initialize released slots with a live incoming side and zero permitted
  outgoing side;
- keep slack-to-core routes structurally zero;
- clear masked optimizer state;
- freeze or dual-track BatchNorm buffers;
- report live one-state and restored-state source evaluation separately.

The audit uses no trained network. It does not say how frequently the two
drift channels dominate, whether the repair improves H-score, or which
partition gives the best transfer tradeoff. Those are Part 11 and Part 12
questions.

## The central conclusion

DEFT's most defensible theorem is a routing theorem.

Under its stated structural assumptions, a severed upstream-slack to
downstream-core edge stays zero, so dynamic slack variation cannot cross that
edge. That is useful.

But HOPE's Eq. 2 neuron owns more than that protected route. It includes a
complete outgoing vector, and its inference map includes BatchNorm state.
Destination elasticity can change core-to-slack outgoing components. Target
forward passes can change running buffers. The reported source evaluation then
restores task-specific state when measuring source retention.

The correct boundary is therefore:

> Narrow routing is protected. Complete Eq. 2 operator immutability is not.

Once that distinction is explicit, DEFT becomes implementable in a way that
can be tested: one partition, one state-transition table, explicit released
slots, explicit buffer ownership, and separate live-state and restored-state
evaluation.
